newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romanian Orthodox church slams homosexuality.
newsitem.headline: Romanian Orthodox church slams homosexuality.

text.p: Romania's mainstream Orthodox Church on Friday denounced homosexuality as one of a series of scourges afflicting the ex-communist country.

An Easter message from Patriarch Teoctist made public on Friday denounced drug abuse, "baby-murdering mothers," a reference to abortion, and "unnatural sins and debauchery", an oblique reference to homosexuality.

The message, to be read in churches on the eve of Easter, April 27 under the Orthodox calendar, criticised parliament for lifting a formal ban on homosexual relations last year despite what it said was overwhelming public opinion against the move.
"Our church intervened to the legislative authorities to prevent legalisation of such abnormality," the message said.

In seven years of democratic change since the 1989 fall of communism, many restrictive laws have been lifted, including a ban on abortion imposed by communist dictator Nicolae Ceausescu with the aim of promoting Romania's birth rate.
But homosexuals in Romania remain the target of discrimination on the fringes of society. Gay pubs are non-existent and discussion groups are kept in the shadows.
Last year's changes to the criminal code formally legalised homosexuality but still provided for up to five years in prison for offenders causing "a public scandal".
Penalties for crimes involving homosexual defendants, including rape and unlawful sex with minors, are much tougher than for heterosexuals.

The Orthodox church claims at least the nominal allegiance of 86 percent of Romania's 22 million people and the country's newly-elected centrist leaders frequently appear in public with senior clerics.
Officials closely associated with the government, including the youth wing of the ruling National Peasant Party, have been among the most zealous opponents of liberalisation.

Western human rights groups say provisions on homosexuality in Romania's criminal code violate the constitution and international principles. They also complain of Romania's treatment of Gypsies and children and legal provisions making libel in the media a crime punishable by imprisonment.

The Council of Europe's parliamentary assembly is expected to decide next week whether to end human rights monitoring of Romania, with proponents of the move pointing to the peaceful transfer of power after last November's elections.
"No matter how great the danger might be of Romania being kept out of the European Union, the Church will always condemn these sins," a spokesman for the patriarch's Office said by telephone.
